scenarios.title: What Does 755 Mean?
scenarios.situation: A deploy script shows permissions -rwxr-xr-x and a teammate asks what 755 grants.
choices: rwxr-xr-x — the owner gets full control; group and others get read and execute
rwxrwxrwx — everyone gets everything
rw-rw-rw- — everyone can read and write
Nothing — 755 is not a valid mode
scenarios.why: Each octal digit is one triple: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for the group, 5 = r-x for others. The ls output confirms it: the owner can read, write, and execute; everyone else can read and execute but not modify.
scenarios.hint: Split 755 into three digits — what does each digit allow?

scenarios.title: Where Are the Logs?
scenarios.situation: A system service crashed overnight and you need its diagnostics. You know the filesystem hierarchy assigns each kind of data a home.
choices: /var/log — system and service logs live there
/etc
/bin
A user's home directory
scenarios.why: The filesystem hierarchy assigns /var/log to log files, /etc to configuration, and /bin to binaries. Knowing the hierarchy beats searching the whole disk — start where the system is designed to record.
scenarios.hint: Which top-level directory's name suggests variable data like logs?

scenarios.title: Kill It Gently
scenarios.situation: A runaway process (PID 4421) has used 98% CPU for two hours, and it currently holds a database lock.
evidence: The process holds a database lock
choices: Send SIGTERM first with kill <pid> — give it a chance to clean up; escalate to SIGKILL only if it ignores TERM
kill -9 it immediately
Reboot the whole server
Run killall with no verification
scenarios.why: SIGTERM (15, the default) asks the process to shut down cleanly — flushing buffers and releasing locks. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored and risks corruption; it is the last resort, not the first move.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the database lock if the process dies mid-write?

scenarios.title: Wrong Package Manager
scenarios.situation: On an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server, a junior admin runs 'yum install nginx' and gets 'yum: command not found.'
choices: Use apt — run apt update first, then apt install nginx — because yum belongs to the RHEL family, not Debian/Ubuntu
Keep retrying yum with sudo
Download a random .rpm file
Compile nginx from source immediately
scenarios.why: Package managers are distro-specific: apt and dpkg on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf/yum on RHEL/Fedora. And always update the package index first so you install current, signed packages from the distribution's repositories.
scenarios.hint: Which distribution family does Ubuntu belong to?

scenarios.title: The World-Writable Surprise
scenarios.situation: An audit finds /opt/app set to mode 777 and a SUID-root helper binary inside it. Any local user can modify the application code that then runs as root.
evidence: Any local user can modify app code that runs as root
choices: Remove world-writable permissions, strip the unnecessary SUID bit, set proper group ownership — then investigate how it got that way
Leave it alone; the application works
Run chmod 777 again to be sure
Delete the SUID binary outright with no analysis
scenarios.why: Mode 777 lets anyone alter code that then executes with root's privileges via SUID — a textbook privilege-escalation path. Fix permissions to least privilege, remove unneeded SUID bits, and investigate the misconfiguration's origin so it does not recur.
scenarios.hint: What can an attacker do with writable code that runs as root?

scenarios.title: Silent Script Failure
scenarios.situation: A bash deploy script runs five steps; step 2 failed silently and steps 3-5 ran against the broken state. The script has no set -e and never checks exit codes.
evidence: 5 deploy steps; step 2 failed silently; steps 3-5 ran against broken state
No set -e; exit codes never checked
choices: Add set -euo pipefail and check exit codes — fail fast instead of continuing after errors
Add more echo statements
Run the whole thing with sudo
Split it into smaller scripts and hope
scenarios.why: Without set -e, bash marches past failures; set -u catches unset variables and pipefail catches pipeline failures. Fail-fast plus explicit exit-code checks turns silent corruption into a loud, early stop.
scenarios.hint: What does the shell do after a command fails, by default?

domains.name: Shell Power & System Basics
domains.summary: Core Linux fluency: text-processing pipelines, archiving, environment and PATH, I/O redirection, systemd service basics, and shell quoting pitfalls. Independent training content; this course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: Find the Needle in the Logs
scenarios.situation: A 4 GB application log needs: all ERROR lines from the last hour, excluding health-check noise, counted per endpoint. Opening it in an editor is hopeless.
choices: `grep 'ERROR' app.log | grep -v '/health' | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` — filter, exclude noise, extract the field, count and rank
`cat app.log | less` and search manually with /
`grep -c ERROR app.log`; the per-endpoint breakdown isn't needed
Copy the log to a Windows machine and open it in Notepad
scenarios.why: grep/awk/sort/uniq -c is the canonical log-triage pipeline: filter to what matters, remove noise, extract the key field, aggregate. -v inverts the match for the health-check spam. Manual paging through 4 GB is not a strategy.
scenarios.hint: Which tool counts occurrences per unique value?

scenarios.title: Ship the Whole Directory
scenarios.situation: You must send a 3 GB project directory (with symlinks and permissions intact) to a colleague's server over SSH, as a single compressed file.
evidence: project/: src, data (symlinks), scripts (executable bits matter)
choices: `tar -czpf project.tar.gz -C /path project` — tar preserves permissions/symlinks, -z compresses, -p keeps permissions on extract
`zip -r project.zip project/`; zip preserves Unix permissions and symlinks identically
`cp -r project /tmp && gzip /tmp/project`; gzip compresses directories
Email the files one at a time; compression corrupts symlinks
scenarios.why: tar is the Unix archiver: it bundles hierarchies while preserving permissions, ownership, and symlinks; -z adds gzip compression. zip loses permission fidelity and symlink semantics; gzip alone cannot archive directories.
scenarios.hint: Which tool was designed to archive directory trees with metadata?

scenarios.title: Command Not Found (But It's Right There)
scenarios.situation: A freshly installed tool at `/opt/tools/deploy` runs fine with its full path but `deploy: command not found` from any other directory.
choices: Add `/opt/tools` to PATH (`export PATH="/opt/tools:$PATH"` in `~/.bashrc` for persistence) — the shell only searches directories listed in PATH
Copy the binary into `/tmp`; /tmp is always searched
Run `chmod +x` again; the execute bit must be missing
Reinstall the tool; the installer is broken
scenarios.why: command not found with an existing executable binary = PATH lookup failure, not a permissions problem. The durable fix is extending PATH in the shell's startup file. /tmp is not on PATH by default (and shouldn't be).
scenarios.hint: How does the shell decide where to look for a bare command name?

scenarios.title: Where Did stderr Go?
scenarios.situation: A cron job's script fails silently: stdout is logged but the actual error message never appears in the log file. The crontab line is `0 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log`.
choices: `>> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1` — `>>` alone captures only stdout (fd 1); `2>&1` merges stderr (fd 2) into the same destination
`2>> /var/log/backup.log`; that captures both streams
Add `set -x` to the script; that redirects stderr
Cron discards stderr by design; nothing can capture it
scenarios.why: Redirection defaults to stdout only. `2>&1` duplicates fd 2 onto fd 1's current target — order matters (it must come after the `>>`). `2>>` alone would append stderr to the file but leave stdout going to cron mail.
scenarios.hint: Which file descriptor carries error output, and where does >> point by default?

scenarios.title: The Service That Forgets
scenarios.situation: A custom app started with `nohup ./app &` dies on every reboot and has no log rotation. The team wants it managed like a real service.
choices: Write a systemd unit (`/etc/systemd/system/app.service` with `ExecStart`, `Restart=on-failure`, `StandardOutput=journal`) then `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now app` — the service starts at boot, restarts on crash, and logs to the journal
Add the nohup line to `/etc/rc.local`; that's the modern service manager
Run it in a tmux session; tmux survives reboots
Add it to root's crontab with `@reboot nohup ./app &` and call it done
scenarios.why: systemd units are the standard service abstraction: declarative start config, dependency ordering, automatic restarts, and journal logging. nohup/tmux/rc.local/@reboot are all fragile half-measures with no supervision or log management.
scenarios.hint: What supervises the process, restarts it, and captures its logs?

scenarios.title: The Filenames With Spaces
scenarios.situation: A cleanup script `for f in $(ls *.log); do rm $f; done` deleted the wrong files when it hit `error log.txt` — it tried to remove `error` and `log.txt` separately.
evidence: for f in $(ls *.log); do rm $f; done
rm: cannot remove 'error': No such file
choices: Quote the variable and iterate the glob directly: `for f in *.log; do rm -- "$f"; done` — unquoted `$f` undergoes word splitting on spaces; parsing `ls` output is inherently fragile
Rename all files to remove spaces; scripts can't handle spaces
Use `rm *.log` directly; loops are unnecessary
Set `IFS` to empty; that fixes word splitting globally
scenarios.why: Unquoted expansions are word-split (and glob-expanded) — the classic shell footgun. Quoting `"$f"` preserves the filename as one word; iterating the glob avoids parsing ls entirely. `--` guards against filenames starting with `-`.
scenarios.hint: What does the shell do to an unquoted $variable?

domains.name: Linux & Cloud Essentials
domains.summary: Foundational Linux, cloud, DevOps culture, and security basics at the LFCA level — filesystem, permissions, services, and cost awareness. Taught independently; this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with the Linux Foundation.

scenarios.title: Lost in the filesystem
scenarios.situation: You're new to Linux and need to find where the web server's configuration lives. You know the command is 'nginx' but not where its files are. Someone told you 'everything is a file' but that isn't helping yet.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective way to locate the config files?
evidence:
$ which nginx
/usr/sbin/nginx
$ ls /etc/nginx
nginx.conf  sites-available/  sites-enabled/
choices: Check 'which nginx' for the binary, then look under /etc/<program>/ — the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard puts system-wide configs in /etc.
Search the entire disk with 'find / -name nginx' and read every match.
Config files are always in the user's home directory — check ~/nginx.
Reinstall nginx; the installer prints the config location.
scenarios.why: The FHS gives Linux a predictable layout: binaries in /usr/sbin or /usr/bin, system configs in /etc, logs in /var/log. 'which' finds the binary, and /etc/<name> is the conventional config home. Full-disk finds are slow and noisy; home directories hold per-user configs, not system services.
scenarios.hint: Linux puts the same kinds of files in the same places on every system. Where do system-wide configuration files conventionally live?

scenarios.title: Cloud bill shock
scenarios.situation: Your team's first cloud bill is triple the estimate. Investigation shows three oversized VMs running 24/7 for a dev environment used 9-to-5, plus unattached disks from deleted VMs still being billed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective first response?
evidence:
Compute: $1,840 (est. $600)
Unattached disks: $210
Dev VMs: running 24/7, used ~40h/week
choices: Rightsize the VMs, schedule dev environments to stop outside work hours, and delete unattached disks — then add billing alerts and tagging so waste is visible.
Move everything to the most expensive instance type for better performance per dollar.
Delete the entire environment and rebuild it from scratch next quarter.
Ignore it — cloud bills are always higher than estimates.
scenarios.why: Cloud waste is usually idle capacity, not unit price: stopping dev VMs nights/weekends cuts ~75% of their cost, rightsizing matches capacity to need, and orphaned disks are pure waste. Billing alerts and tags make the next surprise visible before the invoice. Rebuilding or ignoring doesn't address the ongoing burn.
scenarios.hint: The VMs run 168 hours a week but are used 40. What does the cloud charge for — usage or just existence?

scenarios.title: Permissions puzzle
scenarios.situation: A shared project directory /opt/team needs: all team members can create and edit files, nobody outside the team can read them, and new files must stay group-owned by the team automatically.
evidence:
$ ls -ld /opt/team
drwxr-xr-x root root /opt/team
$ groups alice bob
team
choices: Set group ownership to 'team', mode 2770 (setgid bit), so the group owns the directory, members have full access, others have none, and new files inherit the team group.
chmod 777 /opt/team so everyone can collaborate freely.
chmod 700 for each user on their own subdirectory — sharing isn't needed.
Put the files in /tmp since it's already world-writable and convenient.
scenarios.why: Mode 2770 = rwxrwx--- plus the setgid bit (2): the group gets full access, others get nothing, and setgid forces new files to inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group. 777 exposes everything; /tmp is world-readable and cleaned unpredictably.
scenarios.hint: Three requirements: group access, no outsider access, and automatic group inheritance. Which single mode plus ownership gives all three?

scenarios.title: The service that died at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: A small app keeps crashing overnight. There's no monitoring, and the developer just restarts it each morning. You want to find the cause with built-in Linux tooling before adding anything fancy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first investigation?
evidence:
$ systemctl status myapp
Active: failed (Result: exit-code)
$ journalctl -u myapp --since yesterday | tail -5
OutOfMemoryError: JavaScript heap out of memory
choices: Read the service logs with 'journalctl -u myapp' to find the actual error (here: out-of-memory), then address the cause — e.g. memory limit, leak, or undersized host.
Write a cron job that restarts the app every hour so it's always fresh.
Reboot the server nightly to clear the problem.
Increase the restart delay in the unit file so failures are less visible.
scenarios.why: systemd captures service output in the journal — the logs name the cause directly (heap exhaustion), which points at a real fix (memory settings, leak investigation, sizing). Scheduled restarts and reboots mask the symptom while the underlying problem (and potential data loss) continues.
scenarios.hint: The evidence already contains the answer — which tool shows you what the service said before it died?

scenarios.title: SSH key or password?
scenarios.situation: Your team SSHes into servers with shared passwords stored in a chat channel. An engineer just left the company and still knows the password. You need to fix access properly.
evidence: #ops channel: 'prod ssh password: Summer2024!'  (47 members, ex-employee included)
choices: Switch to SSH key-based auth with per-user keys, disable password authentication in sshd_config, remove the ex-employee's key, and rotate any password that was shared.
Change the shared password to something stronger and post the new one in the channel.
Move the password to a pinned message so it's easier to find.
Block the ex-employee's IP at the firewall and keep the password.
scenarios.why: Shared passwords can't be revoked per-person — key-based auth gives every user a unique credential that can be individually removed, and disabling PasswordAuthentication closes the brute-force and sharing vectors entirely. A stronger shared password is still shared; IP blocks don't survive DHCP and mobile networks.
scenarios.hint: The core problem: one credential, many holders, no per-person revocation. What auth method gives each person their own revokable credential?

scenarios.title: DevOps means no more silos?
scenarios.situation: Your company 'adopted DevOps' by renaming the ops team and buying a CI tool, but developers still throw releases over the wall, deploys still happen Friday at 5 PM, and incidents still start with finger-pointing.
evidence:
Team renamed 'DevOps Team' (formerly Ops)
Deploys: manual, Fridays 17:00
Postmortems: 'root cause: developer error'
choices: The culture and practices: shared ownership of delivery, small frequent deploys, blameless postmortems, and automation of the release path — DevOps is a way of working, not a team name or a tool purchase.
A more expensive CI tool — the current one must be the bottleneck.
Hiring a 'DevOps engineer' with the right certifications to fix the process.
Banning Friday deploys — that alone will fix the culture.
scenarios.why: DevOps' core is collaboration across the dev/ops boundary: you build it, you run it; automate the path to production; learn from incidents without blame. Renaming teams and buying tools without changing how work flows leaves every dysfunction intact. Friday-deploy bans treat a symptom.
scenarios.hint: Nothing about how work actually moves changed — only labels and tools. What did the original DevOps movement say the change was about?

domains.name: Linux Administration Essentials
domains.summary: Hands-on administration: LVM storage, ACLs, static networking, firewall control, journal-based troubleshooting, and scheduled task automation. Independent training content; this course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: The Disk That Wasn't There
scenarios.situation: A database server needs 200 GB more for `/var/lib/pgsql`, but the disk is one physical volume away from being usable — the space exists on an unpartitioned disk.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct LVM sequence?
evidence: extend lv_data by 200G, then grow the filesystem
choices: `pvcreate /dev/sdb` → `vgextend vg_data /dev/sdb` → `lvextend -L+200G /dev/vg_data/lv_data` → `xfs_growfs /var/lib/pgsql` (or `resize2fs` for ext4) — then verify with `df -h`
`fdisk /dev/sdb`, format it ext4, and mount it at /var/lib/pgsql2
`lvextend` first, then `pvcreate`; order doesn't matter
Reboot into single-user mode; LVM can't be extended online
scenarios.why: LVM layers must be extended bottom-up: physical volume → volume group → logical volume → filesystem. xfs_growfs/resize2fs handle the online filesystem growth — no reboot needed. Mounting a second disk alongside fragments the data layout.
scenarios.hint: Which layer sits closest to the hardware, and which closest to the files?

scenarios.title: One File, Two Teams
scenarios.situation: The `deploy` group needs read-write on `/srv/releases`, the `audit` group needs read-only, and the owning team needs full control — classic Unix owner/group/other can't express this.
evidence: deploy: rw, audit: r, team1: rwx
choices: Use POSIX ACLs: `setfacl -m g:deploy:rw,g:audit:r /srv/releases` (plus `-d` default ACLs for new files) — ACLs attach per-group permissions beyond the single owning group
Create three copies of the directory, one per team
Set the directory 777; the application enforces access
Add everyone to the `team1` group; groups are the only lever
scenarios.why: ACLs extend the permission model with named user/group entries — exactly the 'one file, several groups, different rights' case. 777 abandons the model; duplicating data creates drift. Default (`-d`) ACLs propagate to new files.
scenarios.hint: How many groups can classic mode bits name?

scenarios.title: The Server That Moved Networks
scenarios.situation: A server moved to a new subnet needs a static IP `10.20.30.40/24` with gateway `10.20.30.1` and DNS — but NetworkManager keeps reverting to DHCP on reboot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct persistent configuration?
evidence: IP reverts to DHCP after every reboot
choices: `nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 10.20.30.40/24 ipv4.gateway 10.20.30.1 ipv4.dns 10.20.30.2 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0` — method manual persists across reboots; editing ifcfg files by hand works too but nmcli is the supported path
Run `ip addr add` at every boot via rc.local
Disable NetworkManager; static IPs require it off
Edit `/etc/resolv.conf` with the new IP; that's where addresses live
scenarios.why: `ip addr add` is runtime-only — reboot wipes it. NetworkManager profiles (method manual) are the persistent source of truth on modern distros. resolv.conf holds DNS resolvers, not interface addresses.
scenarios.hint: Which configuration survives a reboot: the `ip` command or the NM profile?

scenarios.title: Open the Right Hole
scenarios.situation: A new monitoring agent needs TCP 9090 reachable, but only from the `10.20.0.0/16` monitoring subnet. The server runs firewalld in the public zone.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct firewall change?
choices: Add a rich rule: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=10.20.0.0/16 port port=9090 protocol=tcp accept'` then `--reload` — scoped to the subnet, persistent
`firewall-cmd --add-port=9090/tcp`; the source restriction is handled by the agent
Stop firewalld; the cloud security group is enough
Open 9090 in the public zone permanently for all sources; monitoring subnets rarely get scanned
scenarios.why: Rich rules give source-scoped port access — the least-privilege answer. A blanket `--add-port` exposes the agent to the world; `--permanent` + `--reload` makes it survive reboot (runtime-only rules vanish).
scenarios.hint: What limits *who* can reach the port, not just *whether* it's open?

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Page, Again
scenarios.situation: A service died at 2 AM. The team wants: what failed, the last 50 lines before death, and whether it has failed before — without SSHing around grepping flat files.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct journal workflow?
choices: `journalctl -u app.service --since 'today' -n 100` for the timeline, `journalctl -u app.service -p err` for errors, and `journalctl -u app.service --list-boots` / `-b -1` to check previous boots — the journal is the structured, queryable source
`cat /var/log/messages | grep app`; the journal is just a cache
Restart the service; the failure details don't matter once it's up
Increase the log level to debug permanently; more logs always help
scenarios.why: journalctl queries the structured journal by unit, priority, and time range — far faster than grepping flat files, and it correlates across boots. Permanent debug logging drowns the signal and fills disks.
scenarios.hint: Which tool knows which unit wrote each line and when?

scenarios.title: Cron vs Timer Smackdown
scenarios.situation: A nightly report script needs: run at 02:30, skip if the previous run is still going, retry once on failure, and log to the journal. Cron can do the schedule but not the rest.
evidence: overlapping runs corrupted last month's report twice
choices: A systemd timer + service pair: `OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00` in the `.timer`, and the `.service` gets `Restart=on-failure`, stdout to the journal natively, and overlap protection via the timer/service semantics
Keep cron and add a pidfile lock in the script; cron plus shell covers everything
Run the script in a loop with `sleep 86400`; simplest is best
Use `at` to schedule it once and re-schedule at the end of each run
scenarios.why: systemd timers subsume cron's scheduling while adding dependency ordering, failure restart policies, journal logging, and calendar expressions — the overlap/retry requirements map directly onto unit semantics. Cron + pidfile reimplements half of systemd badly.
scenarios.hint: Which scheduler natively knows about service state and failures?

lessons.title: Linux Essentials — Core concepts
concepts: Everything is a file: devices, processes under /proc, and configuration all appear in the filesystem hierarchy. /etc holds config, /var/log holds logs, /home holds users, /tmp holds scratch.
Permissions are three triples — user, group, other crossed with read, write, execute. chmod 755 means rwxr-xr-x. Directories need the execute bit to enter; files need the read bit to view.
Ownership decides: chown sets user and group; root owns system files. Running as root casually is how systems get broken — use sudo for single commands instead.
Processes have lifecycles: ps lists them, kill sends signals (SIGTERM 15 is the polite default; SIGKILL 9 is the last resort), and jobs plus & manage background work in the shell.

Package managers are per-distro: apt on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf/yum on RHEL/Fedora, pacman on Arch. Always update the index before installing, and prefer signed distro packages over random install scripts.
The shell composes tools: pipes (|) chain commands, redirection (>, >>, 2>) controls output streams, and man pages document everything — man is the fastest senior engineer you will ever meet.

example.code:
ls -l script.sh
chmod 755 script.sh
./script.sh > output.log 2> errors.log
example.walkthrough: ls -l shows the permission triples; chmod 755 adds execute for everyone while keeping write for the owner; the run redirects normal output and errors to separate logs for later review.

pitfalls: Common trap: chmod 777 to 'fix' a permission error — it fixes access by removing all security; find the right user or group instead.
Common trap: kill -9 as the first resort — SIGKILL denies the process any cleanup; try SIGTERM first.
Common trap: piping curl output straight into bash without reading it — prefer signed distro packages.
Common trap: rm -rf with a variable that might be empty — quote it and validate, or an empty variable turns the path into a disaster.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Linux & Cloud Essentials — Core concepts
concepts: Linux follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: configs in /etc, binaries in /usr/bin and /usr/sbin, logs in /var/log, user data in /home — learn the layout once and every system is navigable.
Permissions are user/group/other plus rwx, expressed as octal (755, 640): know how to read them, and use special bits like setgid (2770) for shared directories.
systemd manages services and their logs: 'systemctl status' shows state, 'journalctl -u' shows what the service said — always read logs before restarting blindly.
Cloud computing is rented, metered capacity: you pay for what exists, so idle resources cost money — rightsizing, scheduling, and billing alerts are core cloud skills, not afterthoughts.
Security fundamentals are mostly hygiene: SSH keys instead of shared passwords, least-privilege permissions, updates applied promptly, and firewall defaults that deny.
DevOps is culture plus automation: shared ownership, small frequent releases, blameless learning from incidents — tools serve the practices, not the other way around.

example.code:
ls -l /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo grep -i passwordauth /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl status sshd
example.walkthrough: List the SSH daemon config to confirm it exists and is readable, check whether password authentication is enabled, and verify the service is running. Three commands that answer: does the config exist, what does it say, is the service up.

pitfalls: Common trap: chmod 777 to 'fix' a permission problem — it fixes access by removing all security; find the right user/group/mode instead.
Common trap: restarting a failed service without reading journalctl — you lose the evidence of why it failed.
Common trap: leaving cloud dev resources running 24/7 — schedule them off; the meter never stops on its own.
Common trap: thinking DevOps is a tool purchase — rename the team all you want; practices are the change.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Permission Surgery
labs.objective: Practice least-privilege permissions: create a file, tighten it, and verify the result.
steps: Create report.txt with echo 'quarterly report' > report.txt.
Restrict it to owner read/write and group read with chmod 640 report.txt.
Verify with ls -l report.txt and stat -c %a report.txt.
Explain why 640 is safer than 644 for a sensitive report, in one sentence.

labs.title: Process Control
labs.objective: Start, inspect, background, and gracefully terminate a process in the simulated terminal.
steps: Launch sleep 300 in the background with sleep 300 &.
Confirm it with jobs and ps | grep sleep.
Verify it is gone with jobs, and note what you would try if it had ignored TERM.

labs.title: Navigate and inspect like an admin
labs.objective: Use core Linux commands to explore the system layout and diagnose a service.
steps: Find a config file: 'ls /etc/ssh/' and view sshd_config head.
Check a service: 'systemctl status sshd' (or cron) and read its recent logs with 'journalctl -u sshd --since "1 hour ago"'.
Inspect permissions: 'ls -l /etc/shadow' and explain why it's 640 root:shadow.
Find large log files: 'du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h | tail -5'.

labs.title: Set up a shared project directory
labs.objective: Create a collaboration directory with correct group ownership and setgid.
steps: Create group 'team' and directory /opt/team (use /tmp/team if not root).
Set group ownership: 'chgrp team /opt/team' and mode: 'chmod 2770 /opt/team'.
Create a file inside as your user; confirm with 'ls -l' that its group is 'team'.
Confirm an outsider (or 'other' permissions) cannot list the directory.

checks.hint: The setgid bit shows as 's' in the group execute position.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
